item.title: Trump says Russia 'has been fine on Ukraine' as he makes deals with Putin
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A series of Trump administration moves over the last two weeks — including decisions to lift sanctions on Russian diesel and delay other measures targeting the Russian economy — have led both Republicans and Democrats to question whether President Trump is changing course and siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in the war between their two countries. "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," Trump told reporters on Monday. "They haven't been doing much." In contrast, the president continued, "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given nothing to us. Remember that." Russia and Ukraine have been at war for more than 12 years. But in February 2022, the conflict entered a new, deadlier phase when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine and tried to seize territory. The fighting has since become a grinding war of attrition. The United States has generally supported Ukraine, even as direct military aid has waned during Trump's second term . The administration's latest steps, however, "amount to a major reversal in U.S. strategy," the New York Times reported on Sunday . "The breach with Ukraine has been sudden and perhaps irreparable." So what's going on here? Posting Sunday on social media , Trump defended his actions by insisting that he is "in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine" and doesn't "want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." Ukraine, he said, is targeting diesel refineries in Russia, which is "hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States." He said that "farmers, ranchers, and businesses of all kinds are suffering greatly from this, but Russia is, nevertheless, sending, at a low price, millions of barrels of diesel to the World." But even Republicans have pushed back. "I think it's clear Russia is the aggressor, and we've got to do everything we can to put economic pressure on Russia," GOP Sen. Rick Scott of Florida told the Associated Press over the weekend. "So it's not the first thing I would be doing." When Zelensky was asked last week if he believed Ukraine was "losing" the U.S., he replied: "Yes." "It's painful when President Trump chooses one ‌side, not our ⁠side," Zelensky said. On Tuesday, Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Zelensky in Oslo , Norway. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, participated via video link. On Wednesday, Witkoff and Kushner will reportedly fly to St. Petersburg, Russia, to meet Putin in his hometown with "an updated set of [peace] proposals," according to the BBC. Is a diplomatic breakthrough in the offing? Here's what you need to know about the latest developments. What's changed in recent days Oct. 9: Trump said he had reached an agreement with Putin to supply diesel to the U.S. and global markets. Minutes later, the Treasury Department announced that it would be lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027. Those sanctions — which limited Putin's ability to bankroll the invasion of Ukraine — have been in place since 2022. "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" the president wrote on social media. Oct. 10: Trump blamed Zelensky for high U.S. diesel prices and said Ukraine should replace him. "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump told reporters before leaving for a campaign rally in Tennessee . "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does." Oct. 11: On social media, Trump declared an "ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine." He claimed that "both parties have agreed." Zelensky said the agreement was news to him , but added that he would be willing to pause attacks on Russian oil refineries if Russia pauses attacks on Ukraine's electrical grid and other energy infrastructure in return. Oct. 11-14: For three days, Zelensky held his fire on Russian oil refineries. Meanwhile, Putin continued to bombard Ukraine's energy infrastructure, leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power ahead of winter. The Trump administration clarified that its "energy ceasefire" applied solely to attacks on oil refineries , but Ukraine doesn't have any fully operational oil refineries — Russia has repeatedly attacked and disabled the last one in recent years. Oct. 14: Ukraine discovered that its access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network — as well as Starshield, its military-grade counterpart — had been throttled , limiting its ability to defend itself from Russian ballistic missile attacks on energy infrastructure. "Right at the moment Trump was warning Zelensky not to attack Russian refineries, the Starshield settings were somehow altered, such that the system could not track objects traveling at speeds greater than about 100 miles per hour — woefully inadequate to detect Russian aerial assaults," the National Review explained . Citing four sources familiar with the discussions, the Telegraph reported that "Elon Musk approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine" and that Trump "agreed." In response, Trump denied any involvement, saying, "I don't know if it was anybody, but it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon." Musk wrote on social media that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Reuters also reported that the "order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside [the] White House." The Wall Street Journal reported this week that “Elon Musk ordered the slowdown” — “a decision that sparked panic in Kyiv and confusion inside the Trump administration.” Oct. 15: Zelensky said that Ukraine would resume attacking Russian oil refineries. "That's it," Zelensky told the Financial Times . "The block is out. We're done." Oct. 16: Trump issued an executive order waiving new sanctions against Russia — as well as tariffs on major buyers of Russian energy — that would have taken effect under the bipartisan Graham Act that he signed in September. "I'm not a big fan of Zelensky," Trump told Newsmax . "I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin." Oct. 18: Trump wrote on social media that his "decision on Russia is a very simple one" aimed at striking a peace deal and lowering energy costs for Americans. "Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations," Trump claimed, saying that he doesn't "want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." He continued, "Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way." In contrast, Trump claimed Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did." Oct. 19: Citing "a U.S. official and three additional people familiar with the situation," the Washington Post reported that the Trump administration is holding up "the transfer of interceptor missiles to Ukraine that are needed to protect the country from Russian missile and drone attacks." Around the same time, Trump criticized Zelensky again, saying, "It's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine." Oct. 20: Witkoff and Kushner met with Zelensky in Oslo. According to the BBC , Zelensky suggested after the meeting that "crucial issues of early warning of Russia's ballistic missile strikes had… been resolved." Zelensky also said that he discussed Ukraine's access to missiles and Starlink with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio — and he expected "good results." Will Trump's deals with Putin lower U.S. diesel prices? Trump has accused Zelensky of "knowing that these attacks" on Russian refineries "are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States." It's true that the price of diesel is up about 77% so far this year — putting it near record highs and raising costs for American farmers, truckers and businesses (which in turn puts upward pressure on the price of consumer goods and services). But energy analysts say the Iran War, not Ukrainian attacks on Russia, is the major reason diesel is so much more expensive than it used to be. "The main issue is still the Strait of Hormuz, that there is not enough diesel coming out of the Strait of Hormuz," one recently told the New York Times . In 2025, Russian diesel exports accounted for roughly 9% of the global diesel trade — or about 700,000 barrels a day, according to S&P Global Energy. That number has fallen to about 140,000 barrels a day since Ukraine started targeting Russian oil refineries. Trump's deal with Putin would amount to another 75,000 barrels a day, according to the New York Times . That's not nothing — but experts say it's also not enough to make a huge price difference in the U.S. To put those 75,000 barrels in perspective, diesel exports from Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern countries have fallen by 800,000 barrels per day since the start of the Iran war in February. Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, estimated in an Oct. 9 social media post that Trump's deal with Russia could eventually lower the cost of diesel by 10 to 20 cents per gallon. Ryan Sweet, chief global economist at Oxford Economics, likened the impact to "putting a Band-Aid on a gunshot wound." And that's assuming Russia can deliver. According to the Times, "many analysts consider [even] those numbers to be unrealistic because roughly 40 to 50 percent of Russian refining capacity is offline" — and "repairing and restarting refineries can take months or years in the best of circumstances." Trump has been taking various steps to try to lower U.S. gas prices ahead of November's midterm elections, including signing an executive order allowing tax-free purchases of red-dyed off-road diesel. But an October AP poll found that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of how the president is handling the cost of living — and 65% now blame his policies for persistently high prices more than factors beyond his control. Will Trump's deals with Putin end the war? On Sunday, Energy Secretary Chris Wright described Trump's diesel deal as a "carrot" to get Russia to ease its assault on Ukraine. It's an "incentive to Russia, that if they can reduce the conflict with Ukraine, they can get an energy ceasefire or reduce the conflict such that they have diesel to export, we'll allow it to flow to world markets," Wright told ABC News . The Times has also reported that the "Trump administration's talks with Russia about ending the war in Ukraine have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar oil deal that would benefit Middle Eastern business executives with ties to the two main U.S. negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner." "The deal, which is contingent on approval from the U.S. government and the Kremlin, is for a sprawling set of oil fields, refineries and gas stations around the world owned by Lukoil, one of Russia's biggest energy companies," the paper added. Meanwhile, at their talks in Oslo on Tuesday, Witkoff and Kushner were expected to tell Zelensky that "holding out to retain occupied portions of the country's eastern provinces is not worth it — and that there is money to be made for Ukraine, as well, if it would only drop its objections to an accord, even one written largely on Russia's terms," according to the Times . In short, the Trump administration appears to be pushing harder than ever before to force Ukraine to cede sovereign territory to Russia as part of a negotiated end to the war. Whether Zelensky succumbs to that pressure remains to be seen. "I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate," he told Bloomberg in an interview published on Sunday . "I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks." "If the United States will support Putin — it's unbelievable, it's a tragedy," Zelensky added Sunday on NBC News's Meet the Press . "If these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail. And we will not be able to stand." This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/article/trump-says-russia-has-been-fine-on-ukraine-as-he-makes-new-deals-with-putin-will-his-strategy-pay-off-202502585.html

item.title: Supreme Court rulings have been 'destructive to our democracy,' Justice Kagan says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Jan Wolfe WASHINGTON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday said the court's conservative majority has undermined democracy and "created a race to the bottom" in how congressional districts are drawn. Kagan, one of the court's ‌three liberals, told students at Catholic University's law school that the conservatives have enabled increased political polarization by not reining ‌in partisan gerrymandering, which involves states redrawing the boundaries of electoral districts based on the partisan leanings of voters to boost a political party's candidates. In recent years, Kagan ​said, "both political parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, effectively depriving masses of citizens of their rights to voting equality." Partisan gerrymandering is driving political candidates "toward the extremes, because the only thing anybody has to worry about anymore is being primaried," Kagan said. "It is making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so," Kagan said. "In this election, and ‌the next election, we are seeing large states ⁠with substantial numbers of people who vote for Republicans and who vote for Democrats, and the states are going to be tried to turn all red or all blue in a way that I think is ⁠very destructive to our democracy." The court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, in April gutted a pillar of the Voting Rights Act, a landmark 1965 civil rights law that aimed to prevent racial discrimination in voting. That ruling prompted a frenzied round of redistricting across the South to eliminate US House ​of ​Representatives districts where Black voters make up a majority or near-majority, as ​Republican-led states scrambled to take advantage of the decision. ‌President Donald Trump's Republican Party is seeking to retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. At Trump's urging, Republican-governed Texas redrew its electoral map last year in an effort to flip Democratic-held US House seats, while Democratic-led California then reconfigured its map to target Republican-held House seats. Kagan, an appointee of former Democratic President Barack Obama, said the court's conservatives did not appreciate the real-world impact of their April voting rights decision, or their June decision that struck down a cap on the amount of money parties can spend on campaigns with ‌input from candidates. "I think part of the reason why the court got it ​wrong was a lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences ​of their decisions," Kagan said. “I do think in all these ​areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political ‌system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t ​work as well as it should,” ​she added. Kagan added that the June decision on campaign finance regulation has created opportunities for donors to corrupt candidates. "The one place where the court has allowed campaign finance regulation to operate is to prevent quid pro quo corruption, kind of money ​for favors, and the court never seems to ‌see the opportunities for doing exactly that," Kagan said. “I think you know the people of America look around this political ​system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they’re right,” she ​said. (Reporting by Jan Wolfe; Editing by Andrew Chung and Stephen Coates) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/us-high-court-rulings-destructive-013650423.html

item.title: Elon Musk ordered Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, sources say
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A decision by Elon Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, people familiar with the matter told CBS News. The satellite service, which is used for drone operations, hitting certain targets and protecting sites in Ukraine, was slowed significantly last week. Musk held multiple conversations with administration officials leading up to the order, the sources said. He wanted clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. Musk has expressed distaste with his company being seen as profiting from the continued war between Russia and Ukraine. It's not clear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed. Musk licenses SpaceX's Starshield technology to the U.S. government. He said last week the U.S. controls who can access the technology and what level of service those users receive. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk, the world's richest person, wrote on X . Musk did not reply to a request for comment. CBS News has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment. The Wall Street Journal was first to report on Musk's order. The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some officials inside the administration, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications. Mr. Trump said Monday he was seeking details on who ordered the slowdown. "I don't know who it was, but I'd like to find out," he said. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday the Pentagon has not manipulated the service. "We haven't pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to. And that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions, but nothing's changed from our view. We haven't made any directives or anything like that," Hegseth told reporters, adding that "we wish the Ukrainians, obviously, success." Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday there were still limits on Ukraine's Starshield service. What is Starshield? Starshield is a military-grade satellite network made by SpaceX for the U.S. government and its partners. It runs on similar technology to its civilian sister, Starlink. The U.S. government pays to use Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances. There is no working alternative to Starlink, which has put a massive constellation of low-earth satellites into orbit, and no direct competitor comes close. What happened in Ukraine? Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including a throttling effect that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions. Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr speed cap, that is, the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates faster than the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable. Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr. Strike drones equipped with Starshield cruise at 160 km/h or higher, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes. Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr, making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Zelensky said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Shahed attack drones. The Ukrainian leader wrote on X last week that "the Russians are trying to take advantage of the problems with Starlink in Ukraine, as our interceptor drones depend on this connection among other things." Zelensky has suggested there are still some restrictions. He told NBC News over the weekend the maximum speed was 161 km/hr, and he said Tuesday that he'd spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio about "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored." The apparent restrictions drew swift pushback from U.S. lawmakers, with a bipartisan group of senators asking the Defense Department's internal watchdog to investigate last week. "There needs to be an investigation, we need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things," Republican Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" over the weekend . Why have Trump and Zelensky clashed? Beyond the Starshield disruptions, Zelensky has said in recent days that Russia struck Ukraine without warning from the U.S. , and deliveries of key interceptor missiles to Ukraine have slowed down. A senior Pentagon official told CBS News on Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine." Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to seek an end to the Russia-Ukraine war. The U.S. president argues the war is responsible for high energy prices. His administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week. Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire. In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," and argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," as he urged both sides to make a deal while adding that the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin. "I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/elon-musk-ukraine-spacex-starshield-trump-administration/

item.title: U.S. is reportedly nearing a deal with Russia to free multiple jailed Americans
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Trump administration is closing in on a deal with Moscow that would see multiple Americans released from detention in Russia, two U.S. officials and another source familiar with the matter tell ABC News. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner have been leading the negotiations, which are said to be in the final stages, according to the sources. With Gilman's release from Russia, families of other detained Americans hope their relatives will be next They add that the talks have centered on freeing Stephen Hubbard , a 72-year-old retired teacher who is the only American held in Russia officially designated as wrongfully detained by the State Department, as well as several other U.S. citizens held by Moscow on what the administration said it believes are dubious charges. Moscow City Court Press Service via AP - PHOTO: In this Oct. 7, 2024, file photo released by the Moscow City Court Press Service, Stephen Hubbard, a U.S. citizen accused of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine against Russia stands in a glass cage during a court session in Moscow. However, officials caution that while the terms of the arrangement are coming into focus, nothing has been finalized and it’s still possible it won’t materialize or that its scope will change. Asked about a potential deal to free Hubbard on Tuesday, Trump said he has spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin about it "at length" and called for Hubbard's return to the U.S. "I've been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens. OK, let's see what happens. I'd love to get him back. It's time. It's time to have Mr. Hubbard back," Trump said in the Oval Office. News of the potential deal comes as Witkoff is expected to present Putin with a proposal for a partial ceasefire covering energy and food infrastructure, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Tuesday. Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre joined Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at a news briefing in Oslo, Norway, following talks with Witkoff. On Monday, Trump spoke about his dealings with Russia, saying he was "trying to get a hostage that the country has been after for a long time," presumably referring to Hubbard. "Let's see what happens," Trump said. "That'll be soon." Trump signs order waiving Graham Act sanctions on Russia, drawing backlash from some lawmakers and Zelenskyy On Tuesday, Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov was asked about a potential prisoner exchange between Russia and the U.S. "Dialogue on all these issues is ongoing through intelligence service channels," he said. item.description:

Elon Musk's rocket and AI company posted net income of $4.4 billion for the July-September period (Kent NISHIMURA) Elon Musk said Tuesday he would back a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, as his rocket and AI company reported its first quarterly profit since going public, driven by deals to rent out computing power to AI firms. Asked about a possible tie-up on a call with analysts, Musk said he felt he was "tap dancing through a minefield," but that a combination would be "a good idea." Shares in SpaceX shot up nearly five percent in after-hours trading following the comments. Musk said special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla have been set up to study the idea at the request of shareholders. He added that he could not take part in their talks because he has a conflict of interest. Musk is chief executive of both companies, and also serves as chairman and chief technology officer of SpaceX. He owned 48.4 percent of SpaceX as of June 30, according to a regulatory filing, and controls more than 82 percent of its voting power through super-voting shares. He holds about 20 percent of Tesla. The committees have not agreed on the terms of any deal and there is no guarantee they will, Musk said, cautioning that it would be overstating it to treat a merger as a certainty. Any deal would need the backing of a majority of all Tesla shares, not just those cast in a vote, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle." He said the two companies could gain from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and space-based computing. His remarks came after SpaceX posted net income of $4.4 billion for the July-September period, compared with a loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier. Revenue jumped 161 percent to $14.6 billion. The quarterly results follow a bumpy start on Wall Street. SpaceX began trading on the Nasdaq on June 12 after an IPO priced at $135 a share that raised about $85.7 billion. Its first earnings report as a listed company showed second-quarter revenue of $7.8 billion and a net loss of $541 million. The AI division, which SpaceX now calls "Super Intelligence," drove the turnaround. Super Intelligence is US President Donald Trump's preferred term for AI. The unit's revenue rose more than nine times from a year earlier to $7.6 billion, overtaking the Starlink satellite internet business as the company's largest source of sales. - Cloud computing - SpaceX credited new cloud services agreements, wider adoption of its Grok chatbot and its acquisition of Cursor, an artificial intelligence coding startup. SpaceX’s cloud customers include Anthropic, which agreed in May to pay nearly $45 billion over three years for computing power at SpaceX's Colossus data centers. Google signed on in June, agreeing to pay $920 million a month from October through June 2029. The AI unit turned an operating profit of $431 million, compared with a loss of $1.7 billion a year earlier. As with other AI companies, spending remains heavy. SpaceX invested $19.6 billion in the quarter, $16.4 billion of it in AI, bringing capital spending for the first nine months of the year to $48 billion. Its computing capacity reached 1.7 gigawatts, up from 0.6 gigawatts a year earlier. Musk said he was "fairly confident" SpaceX could bring an additional 10 gigawatts of computing capacity online in 2027. That would come on top of the roughly 2.5 to 3.0 gigawatts it expects to have running by the end of this year. He added that power, cooling and electrical equipment were "somewhat of a limiting factor." item.title: Senate Democrats air first ad in Mississippi as midterm optimism grows
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Democrats' top campaign spending group is wading into Mississippi's U.S. Senate race for the first time this year, an aggressive move in a deep-red state that signals a party on the offensive as Republicans look to protect a slim majority. The Senate Majority PAC, aligned with Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer of New York, will spend $1.2 million on a new television advertisement to boost Scott Colom , a district attorney, in his campaign against Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. The ad, first disclosed to The Associated Press, is set to start Wednesday and run through Election Day. "Senate Majority PAC has been watching this race closely, and it is clear Colom is running a competitive race that has put Hyde-Smith on her heels," group spokesperson Lauren French said in a statement. With just two weeks to go in the race, it's unclear what impact the ad will have in a matchup that's been set since Colom won a March primary . Still, it's a substantial investment in a race that's seen only about $8 million in total spending, with Colom outspending Hyde-Smith nearly $4.6 million to $3.2 million, according to AdImpact. Jake Monssen, campaign manager for Hyde-Smith, noted that the spending was coming late in the race. "Team Cindy is confident that voters will reject this radical agenda at the ballot box on November 3rd," he said. Democrats believe Hyde-Smith is vulnerable Hyde-Smith, first appointed and then elected in 2018 , is running for reelection in a state Republicans have long dominated. In the 2024 presidential race, Republican Donald Trump won Mississippi by nearly 23 percentage points over Democrat Kamala Harris, and a Democrat hasn't won a Senate race in the state since 1982. However, some Democrats believe Hyde-Smith is vulnerable, and she underperformed Trump by 6 percentage points in 2020 , the year he lost his White House reelection bid to Democrat Joe Biden. The television ad touts Colom's time as district attorney, while labeling Hyde-Smith a "do-nothing" senator. "A decade in power, Hyde-Smith hasn't passed one piece of legislation, but she did vote to kick people off Medicaid," a narrator says in the ad, which will run on television stations statewide alongside a digital campaign. Harris and other high-profile Democrats have raced to campaign with Colom Colom's campaign manager, Gerard Henderson, said that the contest against an incumbent senator is competitive because "thousands of Mississippians volunteered and chipped in." "We clearly have the resources and momentum to win," Henderson said in a statement. Colom has raised Democratic hopes in a year when electoral winds are at their backs. Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock was the latest high-profile Democrat to campaign with Colom last week, and Harris, who was Biden's vice president, is set to rally with Colom on Thursday. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate and were expected to face a friendlier map this year with fewer seats to defend. But high costs and gas prices amid an unpopular war in Iran under a Republican president have made Democrats optimistic, with the Senate Majority PAC spending its final weeks investing in conservative territory . It's already announced spending in Kansas , where megachurch pastor and Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton is trying to unseat Republican Sen. Roger Marshall. Colom would be his state's first Black senator since Reconstruction, the 12-year period after the U.S. Civil War when the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments were adopted. Some Democrats have criticized national groups for not spending more in Southern states like Mississippi . "I worry, to be very honest, that Democrats are missing a real opportunity to invest in a serious and sustained way in the South," Warnock said Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press." item.title: States are preparing for an unusual election threat from the federal government
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A small group of U.S. national security officials has been discreetly advising state governments and congressional lawmakers on how to prepare for the possibility that the Trump administration will attempt to interfere in November's midterm elections, according to people involved in the effort. The group includes about 10 current and former officials with experience in the Defense Department, some of whom have previously focused on countering authoritarianism abroad. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Their efforts are motivated not by political bias, they say, but a growing sense of alarm that President Donald Trump will harm American democracy by undermining the integrity of the vote to keep the Republican Party in power. Over the past several months, the group has consulted with officials from 10 states, including governors, election officials and members of the House and Senate from both political parties who share a fear of federal intervention, two people involved in the effort said. The effort, which has not been previously reported, focuses on states and jurisdictions where tightly contested races will determine control of Congress for the remainder of Trump's presidency. Members of the group remain in contact with congressional staffs, and at least one state has continued to meet with them as it works to address potential vulnerabilities. "All of them have said we're concerned but we don't know what to do," one member of the group said of its meetings with lawmakers. "The outcome that we hope for is that states would be prepared for any contingencies should they arise," the person continued. This report is based on interviews, conducted over several months, with two officials involved in the effort. They spoke on the condition of anonymity and that the lawmakers and state leaders with whom the group has met not be identified either, for fear of retaliation. The Washington Post also reviewed some of the documents the group prepared for its meetings. Trump has long claimed that a "deep state" of government officials is working to undermine his presidency. Since returning to office, he has undertaken an expansive effort to fire career civil servants and solicit political loyalty from the bureaucracy. Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, dismissed the group's concerns and blamed Democrats for not supporting stricter election laws. The Trump administration, she said in a statement, "is taking decisive action to protect our elections including prosecuting election crimes, strengthening election infrastructure security, and protecting vulnerable voters from fraud and coercion." The president, Bis added, "is making clear that anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable." In their discussions ahead of the midterms, the national security officials have detailed ways the Trump administration could use its federal powers to sway the upcoming vote, covering categories that include legal and illegal activity. Among their concerns are that the administration could deploy troops or immigration agents to polling stations or seek to nullify results based on claims of voter fraud. Their meetings with lawmakers have mainly focused on raising awareness, especially among Republicans, of the potential for interference and on counseling them to be prepared to publicly oppose any such efforts. With state governments, they've focused more on how to harden election protocols that could be exploited by the federal government, the two members of the group said. Their warnings are based on personal analysis of the administration's activities and public statements made by the president and his allies - not access to specific government intelligence or information to which they have access because of their positions within federal agencies, members of the group said. They described the meetings as a way to help state and federal officials secure the election and emphasized that their work has occurred outside of their official capacity as government employees. Still, their efforts indicate an extraordinary level of concern that Trump may use his authority to influence the election or challenge the results, similar to his extended campaign to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election that culminated with a raid on the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. Trump's approval rating is at record lows only weeks ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms, with voters frustrated about the cost of living and the war in Iran. Democrats appear likely to flip the House and possibly the Senate, and have vowed to intensify oversight of the administration if they regain power. Election officials, including some Republicans, have decried efforts by the Trump administration to assert federal control over a process that the Constitution entrusts to the states. Some GOP-led states, such as Utah, have refused to comply with the administration's efforts to access their voter rolls. "The threats that we're getting now are mostly from our own government," Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson told The Post earlier this month. In January, the FBI raided an election office in Fulton County, Georgia, and seized voting materials in an investigation tied to Trump's debunked claims of voter fraud in the 2020 election. Trump told the New York Times in an interview earlier this year that he regretted not having the National Guard seize voting machines during that race. As he has campaigned on behalf of Republicans, Trump has repeated his claims about the 2020 election and that Democrats are attempting mass voter fraud ahead of the midterms. In October, a group of nongovernmental organizations sued the administration, alleging that it unlawfully collected voting data from 47 states. Throughout the year, he has unsuccessfully urged Congress to pass an election security bill - the SAVE America Act - that would give the federal government more authority over the voting process. The GOP-controlled Senate has not done so, as passing the bill would require ending the chamber's 60-vote threshold known as the filibuster. Trump and some of his top Cabinet officials also have declined to rule out the possibility that they will send members of the military or immigration agents to polling stations, alarming Democrats. During a combative Senate Armed Services Committee hearing in late April, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was asked whether he would refuse a presidential order to deploy troops to the polls or to collect voting machines. He dismissed the question, posed by Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan), as a "hypothetical." When the committee's Republican chairman, Sen. Roger Wicker (Mississippi), urged Hegseth to provide a response, the secretary said, "I've never been ordered to do anything illegal, and I won't." In August, Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, wrote to Slotkin and said that there were no plans to deploy troops to the polls or seize voting records. The Pentagon did not respond to a request for comment. In September, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin declined to rule out the possibility of deploying immigration agents to the polls. Speaking to reporters, Mullin said that they would appear only if there were "specific threats" and that such agents wouldn't "patrol" voting sites. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said that Immigration and Customs Enforcement "is not planning operations targeting polling locations" and would only do so if an "active public safety threat endangered a polling location." At other times, Trump and other senior officials have attempted to use the powers of their office to sway voters to support Republicans. The president has promised voters a $5,000 reward if the GOP maintains its majority in Congress, and he has used taxpayer money to air campaign-style ads ahead of the midterms. The precautions some states are taking against potential federal interference in the midterms signal a radical departure from the threats that state governments normally focus on in an election year. Foreign actors such as China and Russia have long sought to influence or disrupt U.S. elections, and continue to do so ahead of the November midterms, the U.S. intelligence community has assessed. Tammy Patrick, the chief program officer at the National Association of Election Officials, said that over the past year the possibility of federal interference has become the dominant concern of election officials she has spoken to around the country. State and local officials, for example, have been rehearsing how to respond if a federal agent appears at a polling place to compel access to ballots or voting machines, she said. Other officials, Patrick said, have been concerned about moves the Trump administration has already taken. Since returning to office, Trump has pressured states, such as Indiana and Texas, to redraw their congressional maps to favor Republicans. His administration has also asked the Supreme Court to limit the availability of mail-in voting, a request the court has rejected. "All of these things," Patrick said, "are being done in the open." Patrick Marley contributed to this report. It names Alpha Delta Phi Inc. and Chicago Society of Alpha Delta Phi as defendants. “The grief that this has imposed upon me is indescribable,” Doe told NBC News in an interview. “It is the first thing I think about whenever I wake up every day and the last thing I think about whenever I fall asleep.” Doe’s case comes weeks after a former Cornell University student claimed in a lawsuit that she was gang-raped at a fraternity party, causing national outrage, and just days after a woman reported that she was sexually assaulted at a party hosted by a different fraternity near the University of Chicago. The University of Chicago, which does not recognize fraternities as official student organizations, said in a statement that it was “prepared to help the Chicago Police Department” in its investigation. “These allegations are very disturbing to the University community,” said a university spokesperson, Gerald McSwiggan. “The University of Chicago is committed to addressing and preventing incidents of sexual assault.” Alpha Delta Phi’s national team said in a statement that it is aware of the allegations and that it “suspended the member involved.” “The conduct described is deeply troubling and inconsistent with our values,” it said. “We are committed to the safety and well-being of our members and communities and will cooperate with law enforcement as appropriate.” Alpha Delta Phi’s Chicago chapter referred all requests to its national organization. Doe — who is not a student at the University of Chicago — said she learned about the party on Instagram and had gone to parties at the fraternity house previously. That night, she said, she went to the party with several friends, none of whom are students at the university. Doe said she was dancing with friends when a fraternity brother approached her. The fraternity brother offered her a shot, which she said immediately made her feel unsteady and lightheaded, according to the lawsuit. She said she had had only two drinks before she took the shot, spaced out over roughly two hours. She described having the “spins” and feeling as though her “vision was underwater.” “I know myself, and that was not the amount with how intoxicated I felt after the shot that I took with him,” she said. “I’ve never felt like that before.” She added that she watched the fraternity brother pour the shot and did not notice anything “odd.” The fraternity member then directed Doe to follow him to a secluded bedroom on a different floor of the fraternity house, according to the lawsuit. Doe expressed her unsteadiness and lightheadedness, which the fraternity member ignored, the lawsuit says. The fraternity brother began to make “unwanted and nonconsensual sexual advances” on the woman, the lawsuit says. It says she “lost all physical and verbal ability to refuse” the fraternity member’s alleged sexual advances. “I remember backing onto the bed because I knew what was about to happen, but I just — I didn’t feel like I was strong enough to get out,” she told NBC News. The lawsuit says that although her verbal ability was limited, she managed to plead with the fraternity brother to wear a condom, which he refused to do. The fraternity brother then penetrated her “without her consent,” the lawsuit says. After the alleged encounter, the man left Doe alone and unconscious, according to the suit. It alleges that other fraternity brothers initially blocked her friend from going upstairs to find her. Her friend found her unconscious and helped her out of the house, according to the complaint. She said that she faintly remembers her shirt being on backward when she woke up but that she was not sure how she got her clothes on. She struggled to speak and walk as they escorted her out of the home, according to the lawsuit. Doe said she slept over at her friend’s dorm room that night. The next morning, Doe found bloodstains in her underwear and went to the hospital, where she reported the incident to the Chicago Police Department, according to a police report. Doe told police she believed the alcohol was laced with something, according to the report. Police confirmed that a 19-year-old who reported a sexual assault at the fraternity house took herself to Illinois Masonic Hospital for treatment on Feb. 8. Doe received a sexual assault evidence collection kit at the hospital, according to the police report. item.title: Ohio governor candidate hits back after estranged mother appears in attack ad
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Ohio Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton's campaign slammed her GOP opponent Vivek Ramaswamy Tuesday, alleging his campaign used her estranged mother, whom she has accused of abusing her and standing by the man who sexually abused her, to urge voters not to support her in the toss-up race. A video that appears to be a campaign ad circulated on social media late Monday showing Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, saying that she loves her daughter, but adds, "Amy has a serious problem" and has lied about her past. ABC News has not been able to verify the content or authenticity of the video, which has been shared by many users online, including Donald Trump Jr. Stephen Zenner/Bloomberg via Getty Images - PHOTO: Amy Acton, former director of the Ohio Department of Health and Democratic gubernatorial candidate, speaks on affordability while campaigning at Bottoms Up Coffee in Columbus, Ohio, April 6, 2026. Ramaswamy told reporters on Tuesday that the ad did come from his campaign and that he viewed it as "legitimate." He said that Acton's mother was not compensated. "It is an ad from our campaign, and the thing that I want to say is that I would love for this race and this election to be about the substantive issues that impact Ohioans, and unfortunately, Amy Acton has been hiding from those issues. She won't debate me," he said. In the campaign ad, Arthur describes her daughter as a "liar," saying, "She lies about her past." "My daughter needs help, and she can't help you if she needs help herself," Arthur says in the video. Arthur couldn't immediately be reached for comment. Deadline passes for embattled Republican Rep. Max Miller to drop off ballot Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, criticized Ramaswamy over the "disgusting attack." "It's not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at 12 years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point," Stearns said in a statement. "After he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," he added. Ohio gubernatorial candidate speaks out after man arrested for alleged confrontation at fair This is not the first time Arthur has publicly accused her daughter of lying. In an interview with an anti-abortion access group in 2020, Arthur accused Acton's father of convincing their daughter to lie. When asked earlier Tuesday if the ad was made with the campaign's knowledge or consent, Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy, released a lengthy statement Tuesday, but did not deny making the ad or denounce it. "We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor," Luck said in a statement. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images - PHOTO: Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy speaks during the Darke County Republican Party Hog Roast on October 18, 2026 in Greenville, Ohio. Luck's statement went on to accuse Acton of "lying about Vivek and his family, lying about her own record, and then hiding from debates," and questioning her actions during the pandemic when she was the director of the Ohio Department of Health. "If Amy disagrees with these criticisms, she should stand before the people of Ohio, answer the questions, and let voters decide for themselves. The fact that she won't, and Vivek will, should tell you everything about who's really lying," Luck ended her statement. Acton pushed back in an interview with Spectrum News Tuesday. "I won't normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is something I'm just complaining about. Who today just released an ad using my birth mother, who I was removed from at the age of 12 for severe abuse and neglect and sexual abuse; my brother and I were removed," she said. The campaign released a video ad later Tuesday where Stearns echoed his criticism over Ramaswamy "Shame on Vivek,” he says, adding, "It's the contempt he has for Amy. It's the contempt he has for Ohio. He's not fit to lead." Acton has been public about her experience with abuse and seeking therapy for it, She has also openly spoken about her tumultuous relationship with her mother. In an interview with the Youngstown Vindicator in 2019, when she was first appointed director of the Ohio Department of Health, Acton described a childhood that was "out of control", shuffling between houses with her mother and brother and the "cast of characters" her mother dated. She alleged her mother's second husband molested her between the ages of 9 and 12. Charges were filed against her stepfather, and Acton testified against him. Jeff Swensen/Getty Images - PHOTO: Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for Governor of Ohio, greets constituents along the parade route of the 54th Annual CDC Parade on September 7, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. A newspaper article from August 1978 corroborates Acton's account. The article in the Youngstown Vindicator describes that Acton's stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was "bound over to the Mahoning County grand jury in connection with the rape of a 12-year-old girl." Acton was born in 1966, making her 12 at the time. The article says he was "arrested at his home on August 4 th following an investigation initiated by the girl's father." Cledith Arthur died in 2004. He and Acton's mother remained married after the allegations. "In the courthouse after they were charged, I went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away. That was the last time I ever saw her," Acton said in the 2019 interview about her mother. "I was lucky that it got bad enough, because it got me out of there." Midterm candidates dumping debates: 'There's no reason to get up there and argue about differences of opinion' Acton's father received custody, which she credited for turning her life around. She then graduated top of her class in high school, was homecoming queen, and became a doctor. Ramaswamy has also been criticized for making comments seen as dismissive of his opponents' experiences, saying that Acton "only ever talks about something that happened to her" rather than having a positive message. item.title: Trump administration freezes another $1.2 billion in California Medicaid payments
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Dr. Mehmet Oz, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services administrator, speaks Tuesday in the Oval Office as President Trump and Nick Shirley listen. (Jacquelyn Martin / Associated Press) The Trump administration is deferring an additional $1.2 billion in Medicaid reimbursements to California, citing concerns about potential fraud in a state program that helps older adults and people with disabilities with everyday tasks. Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said federal officials took action after they grew concerned about the rapid expansion of California’s personal care services program in recent years. State officials were notified of the decision Tuesday, he said. “California has been growing that program 24% in the last three years. That is twice the rate of every other state average in the country,” Oz said. “Impossible for us to understand how that could be so we are taking major action in California.” Oz did not provide any evidence of fraud but suggested the state was paying people too much taxpayer money to help with services that could be offered for free, like “paying somebody to carry groceries upstairs for your mom.” “Many of you would carry groceries upstairs for your mom for free, but in California, they will pay you a lot of money for it,” he said. Read more: Vance says $1.3 billion in Medicaid payments to California will be deferred over fraud concerns The move is the latest in a series of efforts by the administration to withhold federal money from California. In May, the administration held back $1.3 billion in Medicaid reimbursements to the state over concerns about “fraudsters” in the state’s hospice and in-home care programs. The actions have been part of a broad effort by the administration to rein in fraud in federal healthcare benefits programs, particularly in Democrat-led states. Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla criticized the administration’s decision. “This Administration’s track record speaks for itself: Fewer people have health insurance, premiums are up, and drug costs are higher. This decision will hurt older Californians, people with disabilities, and those recovering from illness or injury,” Padilla said in a statement. “The American people deserve better, and I’ll keep fighting against their attacks.” Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But the office has been critical of the administration’s past efforts. In May, Newsom’s office called the action to withhold funds for in-home care programs a “sick” and politically motivated attack on services that are meant to “keep seniors and people with disabilities OUT of nursing homes.” Those services usually cover assistants who help people with daily tasks such as bathing, laundry or cooking. They also provide needed care such as injections under the direction of a medical professional. A 2020 report by the California state auditor found that nearly three-quarters of In-home Supportive Services caregivers assist a family member. Newsom’s office, however, has argued that the program saves taxpayers money, saying IHSS care costs $30,000 a year, while nursing home care costs $137,000 a year. Read more: Medicaid reckoning awaits next California governor after program’s rapid expansion California’s hospice industry has had problems in the past and authorities have tried to crack down on the issue. A Times investigation in 2020 found that providers were billing Medicare for hospice services and equipment for patients who were not actually dying while the industry boomed. The Trump administration, led by Vice President JD Vance, has tried to focus attention on the issue of waste, fraud and abuse as a centerpiece policy platform to bring down healthcare costs. On Tuesday, Trump and Vance announced a $25-million whistleblower program designed to pay out cash to people who tip off the federal government about fraudsters. The program will offer a 1% commission for tips that lead to a successful conviction. Trump said he would be the sole arbitrator of who gets to keep the money. “I’ll determine whether or not the person is deserving, and I will be very generous believe me. We are not looking to save on that,” Trump said. “I promise you I will be fair.” Trump said the money will be handed out “expeditiously and fairly.” “I promise there is nothing in this for me,” he said. item.title: New details emerge about dad who stopped Oregon school shooter within minutes
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
More details have emerged about the "hero" bystander who intervened within minutes of a gunman opening fire at an elementary school in Oregon. Kaylub Giamanco, 36, fatally shot the 16-year-old gunman who killed four people at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Oct. 15. His actions "undoubtedly saved people," police said. Giamanco, a carpenter and father of two girls who attend Silver Rail Elementary, had gone through "military shooting drills" with veterans who fought in Iraq, The Guardian reported. Seeing the shooting unfold, Giamanco "pursued" gunman Griffin J. John II, his mother, Kenda Freeman, told CBS News . Freeman said the experience has left her son traumatized. "I told him he was a hero, he did what he had to do, and that he did the right thing, and that I was proud of him and that he was a hero and he saved a lot of lives." "Kaylub knew something was not right, so he pulled up onto the grass, grabbed his gun and basically stalked the gunman back into the school," Freeman said. "He crawled through a window that the gunman had shot out. He army crawled through the window." Giamanco, who legally owns and carries his weapon, doesn't wish to speak about the school shooting because he feels "riddled with guilt" for not being able to save more lives, his brother, Kyle Giamanco, told the New York Post . A teacher in the classroom had already thrown her cellphone at John, tackled him and fought him, police said. She was not injured. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said her actions likely prevented more bloodshed. Giamanco then fired at John multiple times with a legally owned .40-caliber pistol, killing him just before police arrived, officials said. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek praised the Bend resident at a press conference, without naming him, saying he "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life." Addressing him directly, she acknowledged the toll it had taken on him. "Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well." "I don't think we can underestimate or under-appreciate that courage," Krantz said Friday, speaking about the teacher and the man who shot the gunman. "When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. And the quick thinking to … follow someone into the school is incredible, and undoubtedly saved people." Gun used 'purchased as a birthday gift' The gun used by the 16-year-old shooter Griffin J. John II was purchased by his mother as a birthday gift, according to reports. The Maverick 12-gauge shotgun was purchased legally in August 2026 by the mother of the gunman who carried out the shooting, and given to him for recreational use, sources told CBS News . On Friday, two senior law enforcement officials told NBC News that John's mother bought the shotgun and has been cooperating with investigators. The shooter killed Rhoam Summer, a 5-year-old student, and Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher from Bend, along with two other children aged 8 and 11 on Thursday. Police said all of the shots were fired inside a single special needs classroom. In an interview with CNN on Sunday, John's mother said that "there were no warning signs" and wouldn't comment on how her son got access to the gun used in the shooting. Schools remain closed Schools across Bend., Ore., will stay closed Monday and Tuesday as the community mourns four people killed on Thursday, when police say a 16-year-old former student opened fire in a special education classroom. Students return Wednesday on an early-release schedule, and Silver Rail will remain closed until further notice, the Bend Bulletin reported . In a statement, Lambert's family described her as a native central Oregonian who grew up in Bend and had a passion for playing sports, especially volleyball. "Her goal was to be an educator and teach in the school district she loved growing up in," the statement continued. "Silver Rail was her first job as a teacher. … She loved Silver Rail. This was her dream job. Megan was compassionate and had a huge heart. She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs. She was an incredible sister, daughter, niece and granddaughter. … She was funny and opinionated and she lit up the room." Megan Lambert, 25, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., was killed in Thursday's shooting. Bend Police Department Rhoam Summer, 5, was one of three children killed in Thursday's shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore. Bend Police Department The shooter was identified as Griffin J. John II. He was a former student at the school who had received special ed services, according to Bend-La Pine School Superintendent Steven Cook. The Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians confirmed Saturday that John was an enrolled member, NBC News reported . A 7-year-old girl who received lifesaving care at the scene was in serious but stable condition at Oregon Health & Science University, police said. A 54-year-old teacher, Becky Drury of Bend, suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries and was being treated at St. Charles Bend. Her family allowed police to release her name. Becky Drury, 54, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School, was injured in Thursday's shooting. Bend Police Department According to a Facebook post from her mother-in-law, Drury has already had surgery to repair significant damage to her left arm and will need more surgeries in the future. She also suffered injuries to her right hand, but none of her wounds are believed to be life-threatening. "The good news is she will be ok and we all get to keep that magnificent woman we love so much in our lives," the post read. Her husband, Will Drury, said her left arm "took a lot of damage" and that her right hand also needed surgery, CNN reported . The two other children killed, both boys, were 8 and 11. Their families asked police not to release their names. Other than John's past association with the school, police did not share any information on the potential motive behind the shooting. "Everyone wants to know why, including us," Krantz said. "We may never get that full answer, but we want it." How the shooting unfolded Flowers are placed beside a sign at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Friday. AP Photo/Haven Daley Krantz provided new details about what happened in the chaotic few minutes from when John first opened fire outside the school to when he was killed. According to Krantz, John approached the school at approximately 12:58 p.m. on foot before throwing his gun over an exterior fence and climbing onto the school's property. A driver in a red pickup truck spotted John and "verbally confronted" him from inside their vehicle. John fired at least three rounds at the truck before heading inside. The driver, who was unhurt, quickly called 911 to alert police. John then walked around the outside of the school and fired multiple rounds into the glass panes of an exterior door to gain access to the school. He then turned left into a special education classroom and immediately began firing. In total, John fired as many as 15 rounds, Krantz said. Officers arrived at the scene within three minutes of the first 911 call. "Seconds later, officers reported the suspect had been shot and killed, possibly by a bystander," police wrote in an incident report on Thursday. Officers then cleared the school, and all students and staff were transported to a nearby church for reunification with families and guardians. According to Krantz, John was carrying an additional 44 rounds of ammunition when he was killed. Police had initially said that the three children who were killed and the one who was injured were the only students in the classroom at the time of the shooting. But on Monday, they confirmed that a fifth student had been present. That student was "physically unharmed by the assailant," a spokesman for the school district told the Oregonian . A fourth adult, a special education staff member who was also unharmed, was also in the room, police said. Investigators have searched John's home and plan to keep control of the school until at least Tuesday to finish collecting evidence, police said. They are asking anyone with video of a teenage boy in black clothing and a black backpack near Third Street, Brosterhous Road or the school between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. Thursday to submit it. The FBI has set up a tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI and fbi.gov/silverrailschool . 'Rhoam was so so strong' People leave a family reunification area following a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Thursday. AP Photo/Joe Kline Rhoam Summer's parents, Kelik and Lillian, released a new statement on Monday through their attorneys providing more details on who he was and how best to honor his memory. "Rhoam was so so strong. The day he was born, his father gave him his first sink bath at the hospital. In the sink, Rhoam grabbed his dad's hands and pulled himself up with his own strength. He climbed a ladder (3 step stool) when he was just 6 months old. He never stopped moving. He never stopped climbing. He could do anything," they wrote in the statement shared by the law firm Dwyer Williams & Cherkoss. A GoFundMe set up by friends of the family, one of 10 fundraisers that the site has verified to support those connected to the shooting, has raised more than $187,000 as of Tuesday. In their statement, the Summers said another way to remember Rhoam is to embody the spirit he lived with. "If people want to memorialize our little Rhoam, we request you draw. Sharks, dinosaurs, monsters... Rhoam loved to tell stories of creatures with big teeth who needed understanding and friendship. Please make art for him. Draw or paint. Use your hands if you can. Get messy," they wrote. Dwyer Williams & Cherkoss is one of three law firms the Summers have reportedly hired to "preserve and protect Rhoam's memory and investigate possible legal claims arising from the mass school shooting," according to the Salem Statesman Journal . "Senseless, barbaric, and depraved? Yes. But was it foreseeable and thus preventable?" Tim Williams, cocounsel on the investigation, told the paper. "That's what we will find out. While law enforcement handles the criminal prosecution, we will be investigating any systemic failures that may have allowed this tragedy to happen. We are committed to holding all responsible parties accountable to ensure a tragedy like this never happens again and justice is done in Rhoam's name."
